adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The modern weather service owes much to a scattered network of volunteer observers, most of whom never met one another and received nothing more than a printed form and a small brass rain gauge. In the eighteen-eighties a physician in a hill town began recording temperature three times a day, noting cloud cover in the margin, and mailing the sheets to a state office that filed them in wooden cabinets. Those cabinets survived two fires and a flood, and when a graduate student opened them ninety years later she found a continuous record of snowfall that no surviving instrument in the region could otherwise provide. Archivists now treat such runs of paper as instruments in their own right, because a careful observer with a cheap gauge will often outperform an expensive sensor that is never cleaned, never levelled and never moved out of the shade.

The same lesson appears in the early history of upper-air observation. Kites carried thermometers aloft before aeroplanes did, and the first trustworthy soundings of the lower atmosphere came from box kites flown from a shed on a windy headland. The operator let out line until the kite reached a chosen angle, waited, hauled it back hand over hand, and wrote the reading beside the time of day. When an aeroplane finally replaced the kite the numbers improved, but the habit of recording did not change, because the pilot still scribbled a short coded message on landing and the code was designed so that a tired clerk could read it at a glance without stopping to think.

That code is still in use. Every aviation forecast begins with a routine observation, and student pilots learn in their first week that the term METAR stands for Meteorological Aerodrome Report, a coded summary issued on the hour that packs wind, visibility, cloud and temperature into a single terse line. The format looks cryptic to a passenger staring out of a cabin window, but it is deliberately rigid, because ambiguity in an aerodrome report can be very expensive indeed. Decoding one becomes automatic with practice, and most pilots can read the whole line in a few seconds and then forget about it until the next briefing.

Forecasters have added many layers since those first kite flights. Radar, satellite imagery and dense networks of automatic stations now feed a single model that updates every few hours, and yet the oldest part of the system, the human observation, still supplies the ground truth against which everything else is checked. When an automatic station drifts out of calibration, or a radar beam is bent by a temperature inversion, it is the observer with a thermometer and a notebook who notices first. That is why the training manual spends so many pages on the care of simple instruments, and why a station that reports faithfully for thirty years is still considered more valuable than one that reports brilliantly for three.

The records themselves have become a quiet scientific resource. Climatologists reconstruct old storms from daily entries that were never intended for anything more ambitious than a local newspaper, and historians read the same pages for evidence of harvests, epidemics and the slow arrival of spring. A single missing year can ruin a long series, which is why archivists chase stray volumes through attics and county sales with the persistence of detectives. The paper itself is often brittle, the ink faded, the handwriting hurried, and yet the numbers continue to speak across a century with a clarity that no summary can match.
